title: Dysregulation of SIRT1, polyamines and miRNA editing in cancer and aging

sections.abstract:
Interest in RNA editing has emerged in molecular medicine due to its widespread dysregulation and therapeutic potential. Its regulatory mechanisms in governing non-coding RNAs, especially microRNAs (miRNAs) remain largely unresolved. Emerging evidence in diseases reveals a functional convergence between miRNAs and polyamine metabolism, two systems traditionally studied separately. miRNAs serve as primary substrates for adenosine deaminase acting on RNA (ADAR) which could regulate polyamine metabolism via the sirtuin (SIRT1)-p53 axis, forming a disease-relevant loop. Indeed, in many proliferative malignancies, hyper-editing of miRNAs coincides with high polyamine levels and promotes SIRT1-mediated p53 deacetylation. Conversely, in many age-related diseases, hypo-editing and polyamine loss blunt this pathway. This review dissects this emerging ADAR-editing-miRNA-polyamine circuit anchored on the SIRT1-p53 axis. We propose this as a unifying working model to integrate disparate correlative observations, providing a roadmap for future validation studies to confirm its potential for combinatorial therapeutic targets and diagnostic biomarkers.

The scheme merges correlative data: cancers display high ADAR activity, hyper-edited miRNAs and elevated polyamines, whereas aging shows the opposite trend. Whether these edited miRNAs causally shape polyamine levels via the SIRT1-p53 axis remains experimentally untested. The diagram therefore depicts a working model linking ADAR editing, SIRT1-p53 signaling and polyamine regulators of biosynthesis/autophagy. The solid red arrows trace the primary regulatory axis synthesized from the reviewed evidence (from ADAR to p53, to polyamine), while the dashed green arrows indicate a potential feedback loop from polyamines back to the editing machinery that is currently supported by more limited data

Keywords: Polyamines, ADAR, SIRT1, P53, MiRNA editing
sections.introduction:
Post-transcriptional modifications, especially RNA editing, dynamically reshape the transcriptome, to govern cellular homeostasis and diseases. Adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) editing, catalyzed by adenosine deaminase acting on RNA (ADAR), is the most common and frequently targets non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) (Hundley et al. 2010 ; Morse et al. 1999 ). They constitute the majority of the genomic RNA transcriptome, whereas only 2% of transcripts encode proteins (Park et al. 2022 ). Among ncRNAs, microRNAs (miRNAs) are the most studied class. They are small, non-coding RNAs that regulate gene expression by binding to the 3’ untranslated regions of target mRNAs leading to their degradation or translation inhibition (Bartel 2004 ). ADARs can edit double-stranded miRNA precursors, thereby altering their biogenesis or target specificity (Kawahara, Zinshteyn, Sethupathy, et al. 2007 ; Yang et al. 2006 ). Recent evidence shows a functional crosstalk between miRNAs and polyamine metabolism, forming a new regulatory axis (Rossi et al. 2024 ). Polyamines are fundamental RNA-binding molecules (Matthews 1993 ; Lightfoot et al. 2014 ) that are predominantly upregulated in cancer to fuel cell cycling (Novita Sari et al. 2021 ) but functionally depleted in various age-related diseases (Madeo et al. 2018 ). These diseases are also associated with altered sirtuin (SIRT1) activity. SIRT1 is a key deacetylase that regulates the tumor-suppressor protein p53, forming a regulatory node in cancer and senescence (Yi et al. 2010 ). SIRT1 level is often elevated in cancer, where they inhibit p53-dependent apoptosis, but reduced in age-related diseases (Ong et al. 2018 ), contributing to senescence-associated dysregulation (Imai et al. 2014 ). Both ADAR-mediated editing and polyamine metabolism are co-dysregulated in these conditions (Gallo et al. 2017 ; Hideyama et al. 2012 ), suggesting a shared pathogenic network mediated by the miRNA-SIRT1-axis.

This review assembles correlative findings into a testable working model in which ADAR-edited miRNAs and polyamines form a feedback loop via the SIRT1-p53 axis; by mapping how this circuit operates in cancer and aging, we aim to guide future validation studies to inform the development of new diagnostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets.
sections.conclusion:
This review delineates a convergent axis in which ADAR-edited miRNAs tune the SIRT1-p53 hub, driving either the autophagy dysregulation associated with polyamine deficiency in aging, or the reprogrammed polyamine biosynthesis and catabolism observed in cancers. Importantly, polyamines are not merely metabolic end-products. SPD supplementation actively promotes the core autophagy pathway and improves lifespan in age-related pathologies (Đorđievski et al. 2023 ). In cancer, polyamines auto-regulate their own synthesis via the OAZ1 + 1 ribosomal frameshift and serve as critical RNA-binding regulators that shape the tumor microenvironment (Holbert et al. 2024 ). Polyamines are also known to physically stabilize the double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) hairpins and Z-RNA motifs required for efficient ADAR binding and A-to-I modification (Matthews 1993 ). This interaction implies a potential mechanical coupling: specifically, the ADAR1-p150 isoform relies on its Z-alpha domain to bind Z-form RNA, a conformation thermodynamically stabilized by SPD (Rich et al. 2003 ). Therefore, the critical exhaustion of polyamines observed in aging may destabilize these RNA structures, impairing ADAR1 recruitment and exacerbating the functional loss of SIRT1. However, direct experimental proof that they feedback to enhance ADAR catalytic activity or expression is currently lacking. In vitro studies indicate that ADAR1 overexpression alone is insufficient to drive cancer, suggesting that RNA editing operates as a context-dependent responder to the tumor microenvironment rather than as an autonomous initiator (Mendez Ruiz et al. 2023 ). Consequently, pending causal evidence for a reciprocal loop, we propose a hierarchical model defined as ADAR regulating polyamines, while acknowledging that a potential polyamine-to-ADAR feedback loop remains a plausible mechanistic possibility.

Crucially, the "aging" phenotype is complex. While a synchronous decline in ADAR editing, SIRT1 activity, and polyamine levels characterizes both physiological senescence and broad age-associated pathologies (Gallo et al. 2017 ; Madeo et al. 2018 ), specific neurodegenerative conditions can exhibit metabolic paradoxes. In Alzheimer's disease, the upstream regulators follow the dominant aging trend where RNA editing is significantly reduced, particularly in the hippocampus (Crooke et al. 2022 ; Khermesh et al. 2016 ) and SIRT1 levels are depleted in parallel with tau accumulation (Julien et al. 2009 ). However, the polyamine part deviates. Alzheimer's disease is marked by a paradoxical accumulation of specific polyamines including PUT and SPM (Paik et al. 2006 ). AZIN2 is also aberrantly increased, precipitating tau neuropathology (Sandusky-Beltran et al. 2021 ). This likely reflects a failed compensatory response. On one hand, SIRT1 loss prevents p53 deacetylation, thereby promoting SAT1-mediated catabolism (Minois et al. 2011 ). On the other, aberrant AZIN2 levels drive unchecked synthesis. This creates a toxic metabolic turnover producing high levels of SAT1 product (N1-acetylspermine) and PUT which generates oxidative byproducts exacerbating protein aggregation rather than restoring cellular homeostasis (Paik et al. 2006 ).

Therefore, the model presented here serves as a mechanistic model for malignant proliferation versus age-related degeneration, identifying the dominant trends that link these two biological states while accounting for disease-specific metabolic dysregulation. To conclude, dysregulated miRNAs and altered polyamine signatures could serve as potential diagnostic biomarkers for both cancer and age-related diseases. Therapeutically, a combination approach using miRNA mimics/antagomirs, polyamine modulators, RNA-editing inhibitors, and SIRT1 activators/blockers might provide a rational basis for treatment. Future studies targeting this crosstalk would be of great interest to validate this model and to flip the regulatory switch between healthy and pathologic states in aging and cancer.
